Prevention: Uproot and burn cotton plants and stalks by 30th
Karonga where uprooting and burning should be completed by 31st
This prevents the carryover of mealybugs to the next season and reduces the use of nutrients by the plant from the soil.
Avoid ratooning of cotton plants because this provides food and shelter to the mealybugs for the next season and also produces poor quality seed cotton.
Weed the fields and surrounding areas, especially congress grass and
Xanthium as they are alternative hosts for the mealybugs, and destroy by burning.
Plant maize or pigeon peas around the cotton field as a border crop which offers least support for the growth and multiplication of mealybugs.
Monitoring: Monitor throughout the growing season for the presence of mealybugs.
Female mealybugs are oval, ranging from 2-5mm long and 2-4mm wide and are covered in a white waxy powder.
Check for mealybugs under leaves and inside bracts at the vegetative stage.
At maturity, check inside bracts of squares and bolls at boll formation and on upper tips and leaves.
Look for distorted terminals, stunted plants with thick, curly leaves, brown underneath and red on top.
Leaves and bracts turn brown and drop.
In severe cases, plant death occurs.
Apply controls when: 25 mealybugs per plant at seedling stage, 110 mealybugs per plant at squaring stage and 150 mealybugs per plant at boll formation are seen
Direct Control: If a small number of cotton plants are infested, uproot and bury nearby where the plants were uprooted
this will avoid transmission of the pests to clean plants.

Restrictions: Use personal protective equipment when handling and applying pesticides, follow the label recommendations.
Do not eat, drink, smoke when mixing or applying pesticides.
Re-entry interval (REI) without protective equipment 40 days and witholding period (WHP) before harvest 13 weeks
